L0@P0: The Pentagram map: a discrete integrable system
L1@P0: Valentin Ovsienko Richard Schwartz Serge Tabachnikov
L2@P0: Abstract
L3@P0: The pentagram map is a projectively natural transformation defined on (twisted) polygons. A twisted polygon is a map from Z into RP2
L4@P0: that is periodic modulo a projective
L5@P0: transformation called the monodromy. We find a Poisson structure on the space of twisted
L6@P0: polygons and show that the pentagram map relative to this Poisson structure is completely
L7@P0: integrable. For certain families of twisted polygons, such as those we call universally convex,
L8@P0: we translate the integrability into a statement about the quasi-periodic motion for the dynamics of the pentagram map. We also explain how the pentagram map, in the continuous
L9@P0: limit, corresponds to the classical Boussinesq equation. The Poisson structure we attach to
L10@P0: the pentagram map is a discrete version of the first Poisson structure associated with the
L11@P0: Boussinesq equation. A research announcement of this work appeared in [16].

L47@P1: 1 Introduction
L48@P1: The notion of integrability is one of the oldest and most fundamental notions in mathematics.
L49@P1: The origins of integrability lie in classical geometry and the development of the general theory is
L50@P1: always stimulated by the study of concrete integrable systems. The purpose of this paper is to
L51@P1: study one particular dynamical system that has a simple and natural geometric meaning and to
L52@P1: prove its integrability. Our main tools are mostly geometric: the Poisson structure, first integrals
L53@P1: and the corresponding Lagrangian foliation. We believe that our result opens doors for further
L54@P1: developments involving other approaches, such as Lax representation, algebraic-geometric and
L55@P1: complex analysis methods, B¨acklund transformations; we also expect further generalizations and
L56@P1: relations to other fields of modern mathematics, such as cluster algebras theory.
L57@P1: The pentagram map, T, was introduced in [19], and further studied in [20] and [21]. Originally, the map was defined for convex closed n-gons. Given such an n-gon P, the corresponding
L58@P1: n-gon T(P) is the convex hull of the intersection points of consequtive shortest diagonals of P.
L59@P1: Figure 1 shows the situation for a convex pentagon and a convex hexagon. One may consider
L60@P1: the map as defined either on unlabelled polygons or on labelled polygons. Later on, we shall
L61@P1: consider the labelled case in detail.

L68@P2: When P is a pentagon, there is a projective transformation carrying P to T(P). This is a

L73@P2: this result was well-known to classical projective geometers, but it is easy enough to prove. The
L74@P2: name pentagram map stems from the fact that the pentagon is the simplest kind of polygon for
L75@P2: which the map is defined.
L76@P2: Letting Cn denote the space of convex n-gons modulo projective transformations, we can
L77@P2: say that the pentagram map is periodic on Cn for n = 5, 6. The pentagram map certainly is
L78@P2: not periodic on Cn for n ≥ 7. Computer experiments suggest that the pentagram map on Cn
L79@P2: in general displays the kind of quasi-periodic motion one sees in completely integrable systems.
L80@P2: Indeed, this was conjectured (somewhat loosely) in [21]. See the remarks following Theorem 1.2
L81@P2: in [21].
L82@P2: It is the purpose of this paper to establish the complete integrability conjectured in [21] and
L83@P2: to explain the underlying quasi-periodic motion. However, rather than work with closed n-gons,
L84@P2: we will work with what we call twisted n-gons. A twisted n-gon is a map φ : Z → RP2

L88@P2: Here M is some projective automorphism of RP2. We call M the monodromy. For technical

L95@P3: but more restricted space of closed n-gons) is much more natural in the general context of the
L96@P3: integrable systems theory. Indeed, in the “smooth case” it is natural to consider the full space
L97@P3: of linear differential equations; the monodromy then plays an essential rˆole in producing the
L98@P3: invariants. This viewpoint is adopted by many authors (see [9, 14] and references therein) and
L99@P3: this is precisely our viewpoint in the discrete case.
L100@P3: The pentagram map is generically defined on Pn. However, the lack of convexity makes it
L101@P3: possible that the pentagram map is not defined on some particular point of Pn, or that the
L102@P3: image of a point in Pn under the pentagram map no longer belongs to Pn. That is, we can lose
L103@P3: the 3-in-a-row property that characterizes twisted polygons. We will put coordinates in Pn so
L104@P3: that the pentagram map becomes a rational map. At least when n is not divisible by 3, the
L105@P3: space Pn is diffeomorphic to R

L113@P3: The action of the pentagram map in Pn was studied extensively in [21]. In that paper, it
L114@P3: was shown that for every n this map has a family of invariant functions, the so-called weighted
L115@P3: monodromy invariants. There are exactly 2[n/2] + 2 algebraically independent invariants. Here
L116@P3: [n/2] denotes the floor of n/2. When n is odd, there are two exceptional monodromy functions
L117@P3: that are somewhat unlike the rest. When n is even, there are 4 such exceptional monodromy
L118@P3: functions. We will recall the explicit construction of these invariants in the next section, and
L119@P3: sketch the proofs of some of their properties. Later on in the paper, we shall give a new treatment
L120@P3: of these invariants.
L121@P3: Here is the main result of this paper.
L122@P3: Theorem 1 There exists a Poisson structure on Pn having co-rank 2 when n is odd and corank 4 when n is even. The exceptional monodromy functions generically span the null space of
L123@P3: the Poisson structure, and the remaining monodromy invariants Poisson-commute. Finally, the
L124@P3: Poisson structure is invariant under the pentagram map.
L125@P3: The exceptional monodromy functions are precisely the Casimir functions for the Poisson
L126@P3: structure. The generic level set of the Casimir functions is a smooth symplectic manifold. Indeed,
L127@P3: as long as we keep all the values of the Casimir functions nonzero, the corresponding level sets
L128@P3: are smooth symplectic manifolds. The remaining monodromy invariants, when restricted to the
L129@P3: symplectic level sets, define a singular Lagrangian foliation. Generically, the dimension of the
L130@P3: Lagrangian leaves is precisely the same as the number of remaining monodromy invariants. This
L131@P3: is the classical picture of Arnold-Liouville complete integrability.
L132@P3: As usual in this setting, the complete integrability gives an invariant affine structure to
L133@P3: every smooth leaf of the Lagrangian foliation. Relative to this structure, the pentagram map is
L134@P3: a translation. Hence

L165@P4: Combining these results with our Main Theorem and some elementary differential topology,
L166@P4: we arrive at the following result.
L167@P4: Theorem 2 Almost every point of Un lies on a smooth torus that has a T-invariant affine
L168@P4: structure. Hence, the orbit of almost every universally convex n-gon undergoes quasi-periodic
L169@P4: motion under the pentagram map.
L170@P4: We will prove a variant of Theorem 2 for a different family of twisted n-gons. See Theorem 3.
L171@P4: The general idea is that certain points of Pn can be interpreted as embedded, homologically
L172@P4: nontrivial, locally convex polygons on projective cylinders, and suitable choices of geometric
L173@P4: structure give us the compactness we need for the proof.
L174@P4: Here we place our results in a context. First of all, it seems that there is some connection
L175@P4: between our work and cluster algebras. On the one hand, the space of twisted polygons is known
L176@P4: as an example of cluster manifold, see [7, 6] and discussion in the end of this paper. This implies
L177@P4: in particular that Pn is equipped with a canonical Poisson structure, see [10]. We do not know
L178@P4: if the Poisson structure constructed in this paper coincides with the canonical cluster Poisson
L179@P4: structure. On the other hand, it was shown in [21] that a certain change of coordinates brings
L180@P4-5: 5the pentagram map rather closely in line with the octahedral recurrence, which is one of the
L181@P5: prime examples in the theory of cluster algebras, see [18, 11, 22].
L182@P5: Second of all, there is a close connection between the pentagram map and integrable P.D.E.s.
L183@P5: In the last part of this paper we consider the continuous limit of the pentagram map. We
L184@P5: show that this limit is precisely the classical Boussinesq equation which is one of the best
L185@P5: known infinite-dimensional integrable systems. Moreover, we argue that the Poisson bracket
L186@P5: constructed in the present paper is a discrete analog of so-called first Poisson structure of the
L187@P5: Boussinesq equation. We remark that a connection to the Boussinesq equation was mentioned
L188@P5: in [19], but no derivation was given.
L189@P5: Discrete integrable systems is an actively developing subject, see, e.g., [26] and the books
L190@P5: [23, 5]. The paper [4] discusses a well-known discrete version (but with continuous time) of
L191@P5: the Boussinesq equation; see [25] (and references therein) for a lattice version of this equation.
L192@P5: See [9] (and references therein) for a general theory of integrable difference equations. Let us
L193@P5: stress that the r-matrix Poisson brackets considered in [9] are analogous to the second (i.e.,
L194@P5: the Gelfand-Dickey) Poisson bracket. A geometric interpretation of all the discrete integrable
L195@P5: systems considered in the above references is unclear.
L196@P5: In the geometrical setting which is more close to our viewpoint, see [5] for many interesting
L197@P5: examples. The papers [1, 2] considers a discrete integrable systems on the space of n-gons,
L198@P5: different from the pentagram map. The recent paper [13] considers a discrete integrable systems
L199@P5: in the setting of projective differential geometry; some of the formulas in this paper are close to
L200@P5: ours. Finally, we mention [12, 14] for discrete and continuous integrable systems related both
L201@P5: to Poisson geometry and projective differential geometry on the projective line.
L202@P5: We turn now to a description of the contents of the paper. Essentially, our plan is to make
L203@P5: a bee-line for all our main results, quoting earlier work as much as possible. Then, once the
L204@P5: results are all in place, we will consider the situation from another point of view, proving many
L205@P5: of the results quoted in the beginning.
L206@P5: One of the disadvantages of the paper [21] is that many of the calculations are ad hoc and
L207@P5: done with the help of a computer. Even though the calculations are correct, one is not given
L208@P5: much insight into where they come from. In this paper, we derive everything in an elementary
L209@P5: way, using an analogy between twisted polygons and solutions to periodic ordinary differential
L210@P5: equations.
L211@P5: One might say that this paper is organized along the lines of first the facts, then the reasons.
L212@P5: Accordingly, there is a certain redundancy in our treatment. For instance, we introduce two
L213@P5: natural coordinate systems in Pn. In the first coordinate system, which comes from [21], most
L214@P5: of the formulas are simpler. However, the second coordinate system, which is new, serves as a
L215@P5: kind of engine that drives all the derivations in both coordinate systems; this coordinate system
L216@P5: is better for computation of the monodromy too. Also, we discovered the invariant Poisson
L217@P5: structure by thinking about the second coordinate system.
L218@P5: In §2 we introduce the first coordinate system, describe the monodromy invariants, and
L219@P5-6: 6establish the Main Theorem. In §3 we apply the main theorem to universally convex polygons
L220@P6: and other families of twisted polygons. In §4 we introduce the second coordinate system. In
L221@P6: §4 and 5 we use the second coordinate system to derive many of the results we simply quoted
L222@P6: in §2. Finally, in §6 we use the second coordinate system to derive the continuous limit of the
L223@P6: pentagram map.
